section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: The Concept of a Basis
section_1.content: Define a basis as a 'coordinate system' (a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space). Visualize this as a grid: the standard basis {i, j} forms a square grid. Emphasize that coordinates are just 'instructions' on how many steps to take along these basis vectors.
section_1.example: Represent a point (3, 2) on a standard graph paper; show the paths 3 steps right and 2 steps up.

section_2.title: The Problem: Changing the Perspective
section_2.content: Introduce the idea that the same physical point in space can be described by different observers using different grids. Show how changing the basis vectors stretches or rotates the grid, making the same coordinate represent a completely different location.
section_2.example: A cat (the point) stands on a floor. Observer A uses a square grid; Observer B uses a skewed, diamond-shaped grid. The cat doesn't move, but its coordinate pair changes.

section_3.title: The Mechanism: The Change-of-Basis Matrix
section_3.content: Explain that to convert coordinates from basis B to basis C, we multiply by a transition matrix P. Graphically show the transformation process: Matrix P acts as a 'translator' between the two coordinate systems.
section_3.example: An animation of a coordinate system rotating: the transition matrix P takes the 'old' coordinates and outputs the 'new' coordinates relative to the new, rotated grid.

section_4.title: Application: Why Do We Need This?
section_4.content: Explain that choosing a 'smart' basis can simplify complex problems. If a matrix represents a physical operation (like rotation or scaling), picking a basis where that operation looks simple (diagonalization) saves massive computation time.
section_4.example: A game developer calculating the path of a spaceship. Using a basis aligned with the ship's current orientation makes physics calculations significantly easier than using the global world coordinate system.

section_5.title: Summary & Synthesis
section_5.content: Recap the flow: Basis → Change of Grid → Transition Matrix → Simplified Calculation. Ensure the audience understands that the 'Space' is invariant, while the 'Representation' is flexible.
section_5.example: A summary graphic showing: [Point in World] --(Matrix P)--> [Point in Local Space]. Both represent the same location.
